title: The volume changed what made the old flow expensive

children.text: AstraPay was onboarding merchants from an aggregator managing an SRC network. Around 15,000 merchants needed KYB before they could use QRIS and QRIS soundboxes.

The existing process was designed for one case at a time. A verifier checked the merchant data and documents, then an approver reviewed the decision again. The internal tool also split the review across four steps.
With roughly three Operations specialists and a 2–3 month onboarding target, most of the cost came from small actions repeated thousands of times.

callout: I needed to remove repeated work without making the fast track available to merchants outside this cohort.

title: The scale was large enough to change the review model
description: The rollout target and available Operations capacity shaped where the flow needed to become faster.

title: Inspect the review changes
description: These four artifacts show the original flow, the project constraints, the one-page review, and the Instant Approve action.

title: The biggest saving came from repeated review work
description: The information being checked stayed largely the same. I changed how reviewers reached it and when a second review was actually needed.

left.label: Existing flow
left.title: Four steps and two review layers
left.description: Operations moved through several sections in sequence. After verification, a clear case still continued to an approver.
left.note: Reasonable at normal volume, expensive when repeated thousands of times.

right.label: Fast track
right.title: One page for a clear case
right.description: The required information was available on one page. An eligible clear case could finish after the first review.
right.note: A second review remained available when the case actually needed more attention.

title: The fast track first needed a reliable way to identify the right merchants

children.text: The fast track could not be exposed to every merchant. I reused the referral code that already existed in the KYB form as the acquisition-source signal.
Operations issued a dedicated code to the aggregator. The backend validated it before routing a merchant into the fast-track queue.
This made routing explicit instead of asking reviewers to infer eligibility. Access to the code also needed to stay controlled so it could not be reused outside the intended cohort.

title: Clear cases and exceptions followed different review paths
description: The first pass stayed fast for straightforward submissions. Cases with issues still had room for a more careful review.

left.label: Clear case
left.title: Finish with Instant Approve
left.description: When the merchant data and documents were valid, Operations could complete KYB in the first review.
left.note: The fast track only applied to merchants with a validated referral code.

right.label: Needs more review
right.title: Move into secondary review
right.description: A case with an issue moved to a follow-up list. Operations could return to it, inspect the details, and write the right rejection remark.
right.note: Reject on the first pass did not immediately become a final rejection.

title: Removing one manual review layer only worked inside a tightly defined cohort

children.text: Skipping the approver for clear cases removed one manual control, so I reviewed the risk with the Fraud team before rollout.
The main safeguards were cohort eligibility, referral-code validation, document rules, and the secondary-review path when something looked wrong. The fast track did not lower the document standard.
The point was to avoid repeating the same review when the merchant source was already known and the submission had no material issue.

callout: The fast track only works when the merchant source and eligibility can be trusted.

title: The onboarding target was completed without a major rebuild
description: The rollout showed that routing and review changes were enough for this cohort.

title: If this pattern repeats, the fast track should become a product capability

children.text: This solution was built for one aggregator and one delivery window. In that context, small changes to routing and review were enough.

If the same onboarding model starts appearing across more aggregators, I would turn it into a permanent bulk KYB workflow. Eligibility, queue management, audit trails, sampling, risk rules, and monitoring should then be managed as product capabilities instead of case-by-case configuration.
